interpretation.interpretation: The diagram shows the phases of the Moon during one lunation, with the Sun (SOL) at the right and the Moon placed at eight positions on a circular orbit around the centre. The labels give the lunar age in days: Luna prima (new crescent, the "monoides" or sickle shape), VIII (half disc, "diatomos", i.e. first quarter), XII ("amphicirtos", gibbous), XV ("pansele nos", i.e. pan selenos, full moon, directly opposite the Sun and joined to it by the horizontal line), XVIII ("amphicirtos", gibbous waning), XXII ("diatomos", last quarter) and XXVII ("monoides", waning crescent). The two texts in the centre explain the illumination of the Moon. The upper hemisphere ("emisperium superius") is where the Moon moves away from the Sun ("luna recedit a sole"), that is the waxing phase. The lower hemisphere ("emisperium inferius") is where the Moon approaches the Sun ("luna propinquat soli"), that is the waning phase. The full Moon lies at the greatest distance from the Sun, and the crescents lie closest to it. The diagram therefore explains how the Moon's phases depend on its angular position relative to the Sun.
interpretation.evidence: Written in the diagram: the lunar ages "LUNA ·VIII·", "·XII·", "·XV·", "·XVIII·", "·XXII·", "·XXVII·" and "LUNA PRIMA"; the labels "DI ATO MOS", "AMPhi CIR TOS", "PAN se Le NOS" and "MO NO ID ES"; the central texts on the upper and lower hemispheres; and the label "SOL". Visible: the shapes of the Moon figures change from a crescent to a half disc, then a larger segment, then a full circle, and back again around the ring. The full circle is joined to the Sun by a straight line. The Greek-derived terms (monoeides, dichotomos, amphikyrtos, pansele-nos) are standard names for the lunar phases in the Latin computistic and astronomical tradition, which I know from external knowledge. The names suit the shapes drawn. Step 1 problems: entries 1, 3, 5, 7, 10, 16, 17, 19, 20 and 22 use "above" or "below" for text beside a shape, and these predicates fit poorly, so they are low certainty. In entry 23 the horizontal line is not a separate element. Step 1 also reads "IDES" and "MONO" as separate texts for the lower right crescent, but they most likely belong to the same word "MONOIDES". The Step 1 transcription "AMPhi" and "CIR TOS" probably stands for "AMPHICIRTOS". The smudged word in the lower central text is probably "LUNA".

interpretation.diagram_classification: computistic / scientific diagram of the Moon's relation to the Sun
interpretation.interpretation: The large circle represents the Moon's path or cycle relative to the Sun, and the diagram may belong to a computus or natural-science manuscript, for example one on the reckoning of time or the nature of things. Its layout expresses a geometric principle. The Moon is lit by the Sun, so how much of its disc is seen from Earth depends on how far it is from the Sun. The Sun's rays are drawn as small strokes around the Sun, which marks it as the source of light. The line between the Sun and the full Moon marks the axis of greatest separation (opposition). The moon sizes are drawn with the dark crescents near the Sun and the fuller shapes away from it.
interpretation.evidence: Visible: the Sun has radiating strokes and the Moon figures are drawn at points around the ring. External knowledge: this kind of diagram is typical of early medieval Latin manuscripts on computus and astronomy, which use Greek-derived terms for the phases. I do not name a specific source, since I cannot attribute it with confidence. The exact placement of the Earth is not shown in the diagram, so the reading of the circle as an orbit about a centre is partly inferred.
